column3: Denmark is building the longest tunnel of its kind in the world, eighteen kilometres under the Baltic Sea to Germany, and it is running about two years late.
It isn't bored through rock. It's made from concrete blocks that each weigh more than seventy-three thousand tonnes, and every one has to be sunk into place.
The first went down this spring. Late on the evening of the fourth of May, five tugboats pulled it out of a Danish harbour.
It landed where it was meant to. It also landed about two years behind the plan.
There are eighty-nine of these pieces. As I record this, in October twenty twenty-six, four of them are on the seabed.
The owner now says opening in twenty twenty-nine is no longer realistic, and it has not yet published a new date.
So this is the story of how you sink a tunnel, what it costs, why it's late, and my own estimate of what happens next.
Look at a map of northern Europe and one gap stands out. Between the Danish island of Lolland and the German island of Fehmarn there are about twenty kilometres of open water.
For decades the only way across has been a ferry. The operator, Scandlines, gives the crossing time as forty-five minutes.
A boat leaves every half hour, around the clock, and then you add the queue to get on and the queue to get off.
In twenty fourteen, when this picture was taken, the express train from Copenhagen to Hamburg still rolled onto the ferry itself.
The tunnel is meant to replace all of that with a drive of about ten minutes, or seven minutes by train.
By rail, Copenhagen to Hamburg should fall to two and a half hours. The owner quotes today's journey as five hours in one place, and as four and a half in another.
Denmark and Germany signed the treaty in September two thousand and eight. Its terms were unusual, and they matter later in this story.
Denmark agreed to plan, build and pay for the whole crossing. Germany only had to connect its own roads and railways to the far end.
Most people imagine a tunnel being bored through rock by a giant machine. This one is built in a completely different way.
You dig a trench across the seabed. You build the tunnel on land in sections, float each section out, and lower it into the trench.
Engineers call it an immersed tunnel, and Denmark already drives through one every day on the way to Sweden.
That tunnel is about three and a half kilometres long. The longest of this type in service anywhere is under seven.
The Fehmarnbelt tunnel will be eighteen, which is more than twice the length of any immersed tunnel built before it.
It's also deeper. The Øresund is about fifteen metres deep where that tunnel went in, while this trench sits up to forty metres below the surface.
Hold on to that difference in depth, because it comes back when we reach the delay.
To make eighty-nine pieces of tunnel, Denmark first had to build a factory, on the coast at Rødbyhavn.
The owner describes the site as the largest in Europe, about the size of three hundred football pitches. More than two thousand people work on it.
Inside are three halls and six production lines. Five of them cast the standard elements.
A standard element is two hundred and seventeen metres long. It's cast in nine segments, and the owner says each element takes about nine weeks.
In cross-section it holds five tubes. Two carry the motorway, two carry the railway, and a narrow fifth one is for technical installations and access.
The engineering press gives the outside as roughly forty-two metres wide and nine metres tall.
The sixth line makes ten shorter pieces with a basement underneath for the electrical equipment. One of those goes in roughly every two kilometres.
At peak production, the owner says, the works harbour takes in about sixty-five thousand tonnes of stone, cement, sand and steel every week.
Every element has to last. The design life written into the project is at least a hundred and twenty years.
While the factory went up, a fleet of dredgers started on the seabed. Marine work began in June twenty twenty.
Up to sixty vessels worked on it, and they finished the trench in twenty twenty-four.
They took out almost fifteen million cubic metres of sand, clay and stone.
That material hasn't been dumped. It's being used to build about three hundred hectares of new coastline beside the factory.
The first stretch opened to the public on the first of September this year, so Denmark is now slightly larger than it was.
So by twenty twenty-four the trench was ready and the factory was casting. What the project didn't have was a way to put one inside the other.
A finished element floats, just barely. To place it you need a vessel that can grip it at both ends, carry it out, and lower it under control.
That vessel is called Ivy. It's really two pontoons, Ivy One and Ivy Two, built for this job and no other.
The method had been used in the Øresund, in about fifteen metres of water. Here it had to work at more than twice that depth.
The head of the owning company told reporters the pieces must be lowered to within half a centimetre, and that the work had proved harder than planned.
Getting Ivy tested and approved by the authorities took far longer than anyone had scheduled.
In January this year the owner said approval of the pontoon was nearly two years behind the original plan.
In the same statement it said that opening in twenty twenty-nine was no longer realistic.
There was a second problem, and it sits on the German side of the sea.
Germany's approval sets strict limits on underwater noise, and on where and when work can happen in German waters.
The owner says those conditions make it hard to win back lost time, and could cause further delay.
And then, in the first week of May, Ivy finally went to work.
Late on Monday the fourth, the first element left the works harbour, held between the two pontoons and pulled by five tugs.
It only had to travel a short distance, to a point just in front of the Danish tunnel entrance.
Around noon on Wednesday the lowering began. Ballast makes the element just heavy enough to sink, and steel wires hold it the whole way down.
About fourteen hours later it was sitting on a bed of gravel in the trench.
Hydraulic arms connected it to the entrance. Then came the clever part, which is how every joint in this tunnel is sealed.
Each element has a watertight wall at both ends. When the water trapped between two elements is pumped out, the sea itself presses them together.
Laser measurements inside the element confirmed the position, and the owner's chief executive did not hide how it felt.
The second element followed at the end of June, and the third at the start of August.
By late September the fourth was down, and nearly nine hundred metres of tunnel were in place.
That is the good news, and it's real. Now for the bill.
The budget in Danish law is fifty-five point one billion kroner, set in twenty fifteen and stated in that year's prices.
Of that, seven point three billion kroner is a reserve for things going wrong.
You'll see other numbers quoted. Germany's transport ministry says seven billion euros. The American engineering press says eight billion dollars.
They're roughly the same budget in different currencies and different years, and none of them yet includes the cost of the delay.
The owner has said plainly that the delay will affect total construction costs. It hasn't said by how much.
The European Union has put in roughly one point three billion euros. The rest is borrowed.
Those loans are repaid by the people who use the tunnel, through tolls, as Denmark did with its two big bridges.
So in the owner's telling, a delay doesn't land on the taxpayer directly. It stretches the number of years before the debt is cleared.
I'd add one caution. A tunnel that opens to cars first and trains later earns less in its early years than the plan assumed.
Which brings us to the part of this project that isn't under the sea at all.
Remember the treaty. Germany's job was to connect its own side, and that means about eighty-eight kilometres of railway from Puttgarden down to Lübeck.
It also means getting off the island of Fehmarn, which today depends on one bridge.
German studies found the bridge couldn't carry the traffic the new link will bring. So in twenty twenty a second, smaller immersed tunnel was chosen to go alongside it.
It's about two kilometres long, and the planning papers for it were only filed in July twenty twenty-five.
That same month, Germany's transport ministry announced that its rail connection could not be ready for twenty twenty-nine.
Press reports of a German rail authority document put the build time at six and a half years, which would mean no trains before the end of twenty thirty-two.
The price has moved as well. The first estimate was seven hundred and fourteen million euros. The German broadcaster NDR is reported to put it at two point three billion now.
That is why, in May, the owner announced the tunnel will open in two stages. The road comes first, and the railway follows once Germany is ready.
Its chief executive called that unfortunate for the green transition and for rail passengers, and I think he's right.
Here is the position on the ninth of October, twenty twenty-six, using only what the owner has published.
Four elements out of eighty-nine are on the seabed. That's a little under five percent of the tunnel.
At least nineteen elements have been cast, three of them special ones, so the factory is well ahead of the sea.
Both tunnel entrances are close to done. The Danish one is complete, and the German one has more than ninety percent of its concrete poured.
The next test is the first special element, which the owner compares to a four-storey building and expects to sink this autumn.
In September, Ivy passed a load test for it, carrying an extra sixteen hundred tonnes.
A new timetable is promised once five standard elements and one special element are down. That is two more immersions from here, so at this summer's pace it is likely months away.
One news agency has reported an opening no earlier than twenty thirty-one. The owner hasn't confirmed any year, so treat that figure with care.
Now some arithmetic of my own, which you won't find in a press release.
Between early May and late September the contractor placed four elements. That works out at roughly one every five to seven weeks.
Eighty-five are left. At that pace, sinking them would take somewhere between eight and eleven years.
Nobody expects the first four to be the fastest four, and the crews will speed up. They'll have to, several times over, for any date near twenty thirty-one to hold.
So when the new timetable appears, the number to look for isn't the opening year. It's how many elements a month the plan assumes.

My verdict is that the hard engineering question has been answered. A seventy-three-thousand-tonne block can be set on the seabed to within millimetres, and it has now been done four times, though the deepest water is still ahead.
The open questions are about time and paperwork, and most of them are on dry land in Germany.
For now the ferries keep sailing every half hour, over the top of a tunnel that is nine hundred metres long and has seventeen kilometres to go.
Every source and every photograph credit is in the description. I'll update this film when the new date is published.
